comment.narrative: EMHRD lack knowledge of and skills to follow and participate in decision making processes policy making and budget drafting. They need to acquire the relevant knowledge and skills to be able to effectively advocate for their rights and monitor inclusiveness in all relevant processes especoiaily allocation of financial resources. Furthermore due to low education levels poverty and a low sense of rights entitlement they are not adequately mobilised around advocacy on education health note almost all the advocacy work this communities are involved in is related to land rights. They lack information on how nacianal and county level governments deliver services and the available platforms for engagement and pubic participation. Last but not least they lack communication and unity accorss communities facing similar realities and challenges to become a stronger voice and influence meaningful change together.

In Year 1 during the training on auditing and budgeting A.1.3 EMHRDs worked together to in draf budget allocation recommendations some of which were presented to the National Assembly in Year 2. More of those recommendations will be presented to parliament in Year 3 when the house resumes after the general elections. In Year 2 during the Bootcamp A.4.1.1 human rights defenders from all the target communities collaborated on discussing strategies for engagement with policy makers. Overall for the last two financial years EMHRDs have collaborated three times on various human rights issues as discussed below in details. This shows that we are on track in achieving this target.

comment.narrative: EMHRD lack knowledge of and skills to follow and participate in decision making processes policy making and budget drafting. They need to acquire the relevant knowledge and skills to be able to effectively advocate for their rights and monitor inclusiveness in all relevant processes especoiaily allocation of financial resources. Furthermore due to low education levels poverty and a low sense of rights entitlement they are not adequately mobilised around advocacy on education health note almost all the advocacy work this communities are involved in is related to land rights. They lack information on how nacianal and county level governments deliver services and the available platforms for engagement and pubic participation. Last but not least they lack communication and unity accorss communities facing similar realities and challenges to become a stronger voice and influence meaningful change together.

An online survey of the EMHRDs revealed that 88 28 of the 32 trained people in Nakuru Narok Bungoma Baringo and Lamu Counties are more able to advocate for better access to health and education of ethnic minorities in their counties. They cited the skills gained from the various workshops such as those on public planning budgeting international laws and SDGs as well as the bootcamp as being instrumental in increasing their skills. All these trainings were offered in Year 1. In Year 2 the Bootcamp was implemented which further increased their skills in advancing minority rights and encouraged project beneficiaries to work in networks and speak with a single voice. In conclusion we are on track in achieving the target under this indicator. The remaining work that needs to be done will be completed in Year 3 of the project. During the monitoring visits at least 80 percent of the ethnic minority rights defenders reported that they were able to effectively advocate for increased access to quality health care and education for ethnic minorities. Minority Rights Group staff conducted a monitoring visit to Lamu and interviewed project beneficiaries in the area. As a result of the increased capacity of ethnic minority human rights defenders the community has achieved a number of achievements including having a school feeding programme at Mangai Primary School in order to retain learners in school and prevent them from skipping lessons. Finally as part of affirmative action Awer students have access to scholarships regardless of grade earned.

comment.narrative: So far under the project implementation 50 of the Ethnic Minority human rights defenders 16 have reported being engaged in the policymaking processes at the county and national levels. In Year 1 only 30 of the EMHRDs reported having been involved in the policymaking processes. On this target more work needs to be done in Year three in order to achieve the set target. The EMHRDs will have more engagement with policy makers on wider policy issues. Through follow up sessions at least 30 percent 10 of the ethnic minority human rights defenders have been participating in the County budget making process. Those who have not participated in the forums cite not knowing or receiving information about the dates and venues where the public forums were held. They have been advocating for access to healthcare and education as well as other needs within their respective community. Ogiek Peoples Development Programme staff attended public participation forums in Nessuit and Mariashoni to ascertain the level of community participation and how they are able to engage in the process. They had the opportunity to interact with the community and learn how they are presenting issues to inform future sessions for effectiveness.

comment.narrative: EMHRDs and EMs have a very limited knowledge and understanding on the applicable human rights legal and policy instruments relevant to access to health and education. Futhermore they have little undterstanding of the pubic participation and decision making mechanisms in place. Accordingly they lack the skills and information to effectively advocate.

NOTEIn total year 1 and 2 a total of 1000 were reached. We have not been able to reach all those who received the report to evaluate whether they have greater awareness on the issue.Under this target the project surpassed the target of 600 by reaching out to a total of 750 members of the ethnic minority in Year 1. An estimated 250 more were outreach in Year 2. More beneficiaries including the CHVs are still getting copies of the factfinding mission report to continue raising awareness on issues of education and health among ethnic minorities. A total of 750 members of the ethnic minority communities were actively engaged to discuss the issues affecting ethnic minority communities in Kenya. This happened during the dialogue forums where copies of the factfinding mission report were widely debated and shared. In Lamu County the Awer community human rights defenders discussed the content of the factfinding mission report in each of the five villages of Milimani Mangai Kiango Basuba and Mararani. These debates took place in the month of April and May 2021. A total of 203 people participated in the debates out of which 78 were male and 125 were female. Out of the total 7 people had disabilities. MRG staff conducted a visit to Sasimwani in Narok and Embobut in Elgeyo Marakwet. The aim was to share interact and learn from the community the state of health and education. Through observation we learnt the hurdles which communities are facing to access these basic commodities. This has been contributed by lack of land tenure rights the government considers their territories to be public forest which provide an excuse for the government not to allocate resources for building schools and hospitals. The livelihood of these communities is at stake pending uncertainties on the next move by the government. The women have joined efforts with male counterparts in the land struggle. Securing land tenure rights for these communities will help them to draw meaningful longterm plans.

description.narrative: Op2Ind3: Number of concluding recommendations defining clear benchmarks for budget allocation for 2021 and 2022 county and national level budgets are drafted.

comment.narrative: The distribution of financial resources in Kenya is unbalanced. As a way of example Kenyas military spending in 2018 was pegged at Kshs. 109.7 billion a stark constrast from Healthcare at Kshs. 61.9 billion and education at Kshs. 80 billion UNDP HDI 2018.Similarly country and county level public budgets do not consider the needs of EM. For example a total of 28 of Nakuru County residents have a secondary level of education or above. Nakuru Town East constituency has the highest share of residents with a secondary level of education or above at 49.This is three times Kuresoi North constituency which has the lowest share of residents with a secondary level of education or above. Nakuru Town East constituency is 21 percentage points above the county average. Two wards have the highest share of residents with a secondary level of education or above at 56 each. This is five times Nessuit ward which has the lowest share of residents with a secondary level of education or above. These 2 wards are 28 percentage points above the county average KNBS SID 2013. Kuresoi Nessuit are Ogiek locations in the Mau.
At least 12 concluding recommendations drafted between year 2 and 3.

A total of 10 recommendations were presented to the county and national assemblies budget committees. Sengwer community presented three 3 to Elgeyo Marakwet government Endorois 4 to parliament national and Awer 3 to Lamu County assembly. This means that the project has achieved 83.3 percent of the target for the three years. There are plans to achieve the remaining portion during year 3 of the project implementation.

At least 85 of those supported throughout counselling sessions report to have a better understanding on the healthcare system and are less limited by stigma

In a recent survey conducted by OPDP and MRG it was determined that 70 of those attending counselling sessions report that the support received from CHVs has helped decrease stigma and have a better understanding on access to health system. A total of 150 people who had received counselling were interviewed through a telephone survey as a representative sample of the population. At least 105 individuals confirmed that the counselling services played a role in reducing stigma and encouraging them to adopt a new behaviour which included completing drug doses starting antenatal clinic visits for expectant mothers school dropouts were encouraged to continue with their studies TB patients continued with their medication some embraced the concept of exclusive breastfeeding households invested their energy on construction of new pit latrines for enhanced sanitation over 70 beneficiaries took the covid19 vaccine and over 30 women went for family planning services among other positive behaviours reported.

30 EMHRDs from 3 counties present petitions to their respect Senates in year 2 3

Overall the target of submitting three petitions to three county senates was achieved as planned. However more will be done in Year 3 to ensure more recommendations are adopted and promote increased access to education and health for ethnic minorities. During year 3 three petitions were submitted to the county senates County Assemblies in Lamu Elgeyo Marakwet and Baringo. The details of these petitions have been discussed in depth under the paragraphs below. This means that we are on target with this indicator. Three project beneficiaries submitted their petitions to their county assemblies. These are the Sengwer Endorois and Awer. Each of them was advocating for increased allocation of resources to health and education in their areas.The Sengwer Community of Embobut forest petitioned the Elgeyo Marakwet County government on August 19 2021. In their petition submitted to the Budget and Appropriation Committee they called for increased budgetary allocation towards health and education. The dispensary in Tangul the main healthcare facility for the Sengwer had been built five years ago but was never equipped or opened for public use. As a result of their advocacy including petitioning the county government the government officially opened the Tangul Dispensary equipped it with essential drugs and medicine and posted one nurse to attend to the health needs of the Sengwer community.

At least 68 of 50 34 EMHRDs 50 women between year 2 and 3

During most of the project activities we conducted surveys to find out how project beneficiaries are engaging independently on public policy processes. The surveys revealed that at least 50 of the participants had at least engaged in the planning and budgeting processes. Most of this independent participation was witnessed in year 2 of project implementation. There is good progress in achieving this target. description.narrative: Op4Ind3: Number of EMHRDs participate in national level advocacy events out of 50 EMHRDs;At least 92% of 50 (46) EMHRDs (50% women) between year 1, 2 and 3

comment.narrative: EMHRDs have had few opportunities to collaborate even though they face similar problems. However communities remain isolated and competitive to each other which prevents from stable cooperation. The few gains that have been are not being disseminated or reated as best practices among communities and fear and distrust harnessed through years of divide and rule policies have defeated a sense of solidarity and knowledge sharing among the different groups.OPDP have made some limited inroads into networking and movement building around questions concerning title to territory in the aftermath of the 2017 judgement on the Mau Forest. However the nature of title to territory claims does not easily translate to the era of health and education where intelligently codesigned programmes that take into account the particularities of forest dwelling communities could serve as an ideal policy model for all.
At least 92 of 50 46 EMHRDs 50 women between year 1 2 and 3

Only 20 or 8 of EMHRDS participated in nationallevel advocacy events. They were for the submission of a petition to the national Assembly by the Endorois Community in Baringo. The other actions which are documented below were not supported by the project but they are relevant and involve EMHRDs who had been trained under this project. Under this target we have not performed very well because of the ongoing political campaigns in the country. This has led to absence of policy makers Members of Parliament from the August House where they make laws and enact budgets. However from September 2022 a new parliament will be in place and more advocacy events will be organized so we expect to meet the target. Between June September 2021 OPDP assisted indigenous communities including the Sengwer Endorois and Ogiek of Mau to document historical land claims that were submitted to the National Land Commission. The process involved building capacity of the community representatives who supported in drafting historical land injustices community consultations and consolidation of evidence. The submitted historical claims to the National Land Commission NLC provided a platform to the communities in enhancing their advocacy efforts in pushing for the recognition of their land rights. httpstwitter.comOgiekPeoplesstatus1452535049778311174In terms of progress in addressing these historical land injustices the National Land Commission has pointed out that they do not have sufficient resources to support the demarcation mapping and titling of community lands. However the Community Land Action Now CLAN is in the process of mobilising resources to support the land demarcation and titling process. Security of land tenure is a central theme in accessing health and education for the ethnic minorities in Kenya.

description.narrative: Op4Ind4: Number of petitions on how to improve access to health and education for EM are submitted to parliament;

comment.narrative: EMHRDs have had few opportunities to collaborate even though they face similar problems. However communities remain isolated and competitive to each other which prevents from stable cooperation. The few gains that have been are not being disseminated or reated as best practices among communities and fear and distrust harnessed through years of divide and rule policies have defeated a sense of solidarity and knowledge sharing among the different groups.OPDP have made some limited inroads into networking and movement building around questions concerning title to territory in the aftermath of the 2017 judgement on the Mau Forest. However the nature of title to territory claims does not easily translate to the era of health and education where intelligently codesigned programmes that take into account the particularities of forest dwelling communities could serve as an ideal policy model for all.
10 EMHRDs selected from 6 counties present petitions to parliament in year 2 3

One petition was submitted to parliament National Assembly in Year 2. During Year 1 no petition was submitted because the EMHRDs were being trained. The second Petition will be submitted in Year 3. Therefore we conclude that we are on progress with this target. A group of direct project beneficiaries from the Endorois community submitted a petition to the National Assembly on February 15 2022. This petition covered various issues affecting the Endorois people. The issues were discussed during the Bootcamp activity implemented under this project. The group of ethnic minority human rights defenders who had been trained on public planning and budgeting as well as on Sustainable Development Goals focused their attention on access to education and health in their petition to parliament. First they demanded the establishment of primary and secondary schools in areas where students walked for long distances to access education. Second they demanded for construction of boarding schools under the National Council of Nomadic Education in Kenya programme in order to cater for the education of households who are nomads in Baringo South Sub County. The ethnic minority human rights defenders called upon the security committee at the national assembly to investigate the state of insecurity in Baringo which is occasioned by cattle rustling and recently land grabbing by the neighbouring majority communities such as the Pokot. description.narrative: Op4Ind6: Increased visibility of the health and education issues faced by EM in Kenya and the region at the African Commission level.

comment.narrative: Media coverage or the visibility on minoroties access to health and education is quite limited in the national and regional media.
T6 Media repercussion at least 6 mentions in different outlets and social media

Overall the target under this indicator has partially been achieved. There was a lot of visibility on social mediaonline but no coverage by traditional media was achieved. In Year 3 this will be arranged in advance. Hence this target was 50 achieved. Ethnic Minority human rights defenders across Africa came together to call on African states to take urgent action that protects their economic social and cultural rights. EMHRDs under this project participated in a webinar titled Inclusive economic social and cultural policies for indigenous peoples in Africa. The webinar was organised by Minority Rights Group in collaboration with members of the Working Group on Indigenous and minority Populations and Communities in Africa WGIPM. It was a side event of the 69th Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples Rights. The side event was held online due to travel restrictions of Covid19 pandemic outbreak. The event was attended by 60 advocates of minority and indigenous peoples rights across Africa Asia Europe Canada and the United States of America. Experts on health and education minority and indigenous organisations and regional stakeholders presented and moderated the online panel sessions. Out of this webinar a report was shared with the African Commission on Human and Peoples Rights for their consideration. MRG is following up on how the report was used or adopted.

title.narrative: To improve access to quality health care and education for ethnic minority (EM) communities in Kenya

description.narrative: To improve access to quality health care and education for ethnic minority (EM) communities in Kenya

title.narrative: Oc1Ind4: Availability of statistical data on EMs access to health and education to support/inform more comprehensive and inclusive budget and policy making procedures.

description.narrative: Oc1Ind4: Availability of statistical data on EMs access to health and education to support/inform more comprehensive and inclusive budget and policy making procedures.

comment.narrative: No disaggregated data on poverty exists specifically for minority and indigenous peoples. Poverty levels in Kenya are higher in rural areas than in urban areas 50.2 in the rural areas and 33.5 in urban areas and this directly impacts access to quality education and health Kenya SDG Report 2017. Disaggregated data on indigenous peoples health and education status are hard to find due exclusion of hard to reach areas where they live United nations 2016. Data is necessary to gain an accurate understanding of EMs needs and crucial baseline to address them.
Relevant disaggregated data made available on at least 3 counties by the end of the project

Availability of disaggregated data is still a challenge in Kenya. The available data is from the Housing Census 2019 which only provides aggregate data on population of some of the communities covered under this project Ogiek and Endorois. Under this project more advocacy will be conducted in Year 3 to push for production of disaggregated data.

Poverty levels in Kenya are higher in rural areas than in urban areas 50.2 in the rural areas and 33.5 in urban areas and this directly impacts access to quality education and health Kenya SDG Report 2017. Disaggregated data on indigenous peoples health and education status are hard to find due exclusion of hard to reach areas where they live United nations 2016. Data is necessary to gain an accurate understanding of EMs needs and crucial baseline to address them.
Relevant disaggregated data made available on at least 3 counties by the end of the project

Availability of disaggregated data is still a challenge in Kenya. The available data is from the Housing Census 2019 which only provides aggregate data on population of some of the communities covered under this project Ogiek and Endorois. Under this project more advocacy will be conducted in Year 3 to push for production of disaggregated data.
